newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition agrees cut in solidarity tax.
newsitem.headline: German coalition agrees cut in solidarity tax.

text.p: Germany's government, trying to cut taxes and still make the grade for Europe's single currency, on Wednesday agreed to slice two points in 1998 off an unpopular tax raised to aid east Germany, coalition sources said.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party coalition agreed to cut the solidarity surcharge to 5.5 percent on January 1, 1998 but has failed so far to find a way to finance the reduction.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters that "more work will have to be done" before the tax decisions can be outlined publicly on Thursday. He gave no details.

But Michael Glos, parliamentary chief of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), confirmed that the solidarity tax cut would go hand-in-hand with first measures of a major tax reform which had originally been planned for 1999.
"The first step (of the tax reform) can be brought forward to 1998. We can include a reduction in the solidarity surcharge in this step," Glos told SAT1 television.

Wrangling over plans to cut taxes almost tore apart Kohl's 14-year alliance in the autumn, when a spending blowout threatened Waigel's bid to slash borrowing in 1997 to meet the Maastricht treaty's tight budget deficit target.

Then, junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) -- who have staked their political survival on tax cuts -- were forced to give up on a hard-won coalition pledge to trim the solidarity tax by a point next year.
This time, the FDP looks to have saved face by winning a bigger cut in 1998 than earlier planned, as well as ensuring that parts of the tax reform are brought forward.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt (FDP) said a range of financing options had been discussed to compensate for losses in revenue arising from the solidarity tax cut. "Now the elements must be brought together into a package," he said.

Waigel's tax strategy foresees big income tax cuts, partly offset by scrapping a range of tax breaks. But work on finalising a reform package in a coalition tax commission he chairs has fallen behind schedule.
The commission held another session on Wednesday afternoon to discuss its key points, but Waigel said it would not present its final proposals until late January.

Coalition tax wrangling is continuing against a backdrop of swelling government spending and failing tax receipts which the Bundesbank said on Tuesday would lead to another rise in state borrowing this year.
Germany's budget deficit -- which hit 3.5 percent of gross domestic product in 1995 -- will widen again this year, missing Maastricht's three percent target.
And a strict enforcement of Waigel's austerity budget for 1997 was not only vital for joining monetary union in 1999 but a "top financial priority", the Bundesbank urged.
Ernst Schwanhold, economics spokesman of the opposition Social Democrats, dismissed the coalition deal on cutting the solidarity tax as little more than a Christmas gimmick.

"Peace on earth, and the coalition can start its Christmas holidays. But no pressing problem has been solved: unemployment is rising, basic arithmetic has been suspended, and nothing has been financed," Schwanhold said in a statement.
